id_and_class.summary: John Campbell argues that conscious attention to a perceived object is what lets us refer to it and think about it, as when we say ‘that tree’ or ‘this cup’. On his Relational View, experience is a direct relation between subject and object, and its qualitative character is the character of the perceived scene itself rather than an inner representation.
id_and_class.core_identity_tagline: Conscious Attention as the Basis of Reference

conceptual_ground.explanatory_identity_claim: Perceptual consciousness is a direct relation of acquaintance between a subject and objects in the environment, made usable for thought by selective conscious attention.
conceptual_ground.subjectivity_and_intentionality: Thought gets its grip on particular objects through conscious attention. Knowing which thing a demonstrative like ‘that woman’ refers to is constituted by consciously attending to that thing, not by a causal or descriptive link.
conceptual_ground.qualia_account: The qualitative character of experience is constituted by the qualitative character of the perceived scene. Qualities belong to the objects we are related to, not to an internal model.
conceptual_ground.ontological_commitments: Perceiving subjects, mind-independent objects and scenes with their own qualitative character, and the relation of conscious attention between them.
conceptual_ground.epistemic_access: Philosophical analysis of reference and demonstrative thought, informed by cognitive psychology of attention and the binding problem.
conceptual_ground.constituents_and_structure: Three linked concepts: consciousness of objects, selective attention to them, and reference to them in thought and language.

mechanism_and_dynamics.scope_of_consciousness: Perceptual (phenomenal) consciousness; attention; reference and demonstrative thought
mechanism_and_dynamics.distinctive_mechanism_or_principle: Conscious attention singles out an object from its surroundings, and this attentional relation supplies knowledge of what one’s demonstrative thoughts refer to.
mechanism_and_dynamics.location_and_distribution: Experience is a relation that reaches out to objects in the environment rather than a state confined to the head.
mechanism_and_dynamics.causation_and_functional_role: Conscious attention is causally necessary for referring to and thinking about specific objects, so consciousness directly shapes thought and language. Campbell rejects epiphenomenalism on these grounds.
mechanism_and_dynamics.integration_or_binding: Following Anne Treisman’s Feature Integration Theory, spatial attention selects a location and the sensory features there are integrated into a single perceived object.
mechanism_and_dynamics.information_flow_or_representation: Campbell denies that experience is a representation or internal model of its object; reference rests on relational awareness rather than descriptive content.
core_claims_and_evidence: To refer to a perceived object, one must consciously attend to it, distinguishing it from its surroundings.
Knowledge of the reference of a perceptual demonstrative comes from direct conscious acquaintance with the object, extending Bertrand Russell’s notion of acquaintance.
Empirical work on the binding problem, such as Treisman’s Feature Integration Theory, explains how attention delivers objects for reference.
Because consciousness of objects explains our capacity to think about them, consciousness cannot be causally idle.
mechanism_and_dynamics.basis_of_belief_or_evidence_type: Philosophical analysis of reference supported by cognitive psychology of attention

empirics_and_critiques.known_empirical_interventions_or_tests: Campbell relies on attention and feature-binding research associated with Treisman’s Feature Integration Theory.
empirics_and_critiques.open_questions_and_limitations: It remains open whether reference to or thought about objects can occur without conscious attention, as in unconscious processing or minds without consciousness.
empirics_and_critiques.ontological_coherence: Fits a realist picture of a mind-independent world, but Campbell does not explain how the relation of experience arises from brain processes.

sources_and_references.title_with_names: Past, Space, and Self, John Campbell
J. Campbell’s Attention-Empowered Relationalism, Landscape of Consciousness, Robert Lawrence Kuhn
